chapter: Harlem scene and race in music
title: Harlem clubs for black audiences versus white-only places
summary: He distinguishes Harlem clubs welcoming black patrons from Connie's Inn and the Cotton Club, and after-hours spots like Mexico's.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: So in Harlem there were two kinds of places -- there were the regular clubs where black musicians played and where you as a kid -- that's the kind of place where you sat in without pay at the beginning.
Yes.
Right? And those were for black people of the Harlem community.
They were for black people, but also for any white people who wanted to come.
And then there were the exclusively white places, in which black entertainers and black musicians performed.
In Harlem.
In Harlem.
And which did not welcome the black customer.
Right. And that was the kind of music that was regarded by the leaders of black taste, say, conventional black taste, as undignified.
To a great extent, I would think so. Yes.
Uh huh. And that was the kind of music that was being developed by blacks in the domain of
jazz which had very little connection with the Harlem Renaissance.
Right. Oh yes.
Because if there was anything that black musicians and composers and arrangers were doing, that was the music.
That's right.
And that was something quite apart from the Renaissance.
That's right. Absolutely.
Right.
The development of jazz as, you know, as it came up in the New York area, was what you'd hear in the clubs really, after hours, you know?
Right.

Which is where the musicians even like, musicians when they got through playing down at the Roseland with Fletcher Henderson and playing the arrangements, they would come up to places like the Rhythm Club or some of the late hour places that were big. Mexico's, a place called Mexico's on 133rd street, and places that went until maybe 6 and 7 o'clock in the morning, and these guys would just play.
Yeah, and that was the kind of a club -- Mexico's and all that kind of stuff -- that was the
kind of a club which was primarily for the Harlem community, but where whites could come if they were interested.
Oh yes. Yes.
Right. But that was not the Connie's Carney's Inn and so on, which was for whites and which discouraged blacks from coming in.
That's right. Connie's Carney's Inn, and the Cotton Club, they really did not welcome the black customer.
